results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.draft_locus: Journey SLOs: Defining Reliability Where Liquidity Is Made ¶4
results.quote: counting failed and slow human requests against about 7 billion search requests in a 28-day period.
results.finding: The paragraph ends on the 30% statistic with no sentence saying what it shows. The spec's evidence is meant to show that one peak-hour incident can spend about a third of a month's budget, so the policy bites; the draft leaves the reader to infer that (flow reader A, item A4, stopped here to check the arithmetic).

results.draft_locus: Cost: Making Scale Visible per Unit of Work ¶3
results.quote: partly because its listings carry more revenue; the unit cost should be read against revenue per listing, not alone
results.finding: The explanation of the Motorvane row misreads the evidence: higher revenue per listing does not cause higher cost. The spec's point is that Motorvane's high unit cost must be read against its higher revenue per listing; the draft states revenue as a cause of cost (flow reader B, item B8, calls it a non sequitur).

results.draft_locus: Vertical Differences ¶1
results.quote: The verticals differ too.
results.finding: Declared relationship is contrast, carrying over trade-offs that hold for every vertical and introducing where the verticals differ. 'differ too' frames the section as an addition to the trade-offs rather than a contrast with choices that hold everywhere, and does not pick up the carried-over idea; flow reader A also found the link from trade-offs thin.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶4
results.quote: what protects it (control points with the bot controls at the edge, capacity, degradation, regions, incidents) and what it costs. The evidence comes from SRE, Vinted, Adevinta, Rightmove, FinOps and bot reports.
results.finding: Reader A (A1): 'Three telegraphic lists with nested parentheses; read twice. The evidence-sources sentence adds nothing to the roadmap.' The roadmap's order is sound; its compressed wording makes the reader reread.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B B1 (run-on list with nested parentheses; 'control points with the bot controls at the edge' hard to parse; re-read)

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Forty-Eight Minutes on a Sunday Evening ¶5
results.quote: The "Sunday-evening peak" is a Veldmark illustration; the documented public example of a marketing-driven peak is Rightmove's
results.finding: Reader A (A2): 'Sourcing aside after Ingrid's question flattens the hand-off.' The spec places the Rightmove contrast as the scene's last paragraph, after the question the chapter answers, so the difficulty comes from the order; reader B suggests moving it into Traffic Shape beside the marketing row.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B B2 (right after the scene's closing question, deflates it; belongs in traffic shape)

results.draft_locus: Journey SLOs: Defining Reliability Where Liquidity Is Made ¶3
results.quote: the Rotterdam city bike left search one minute after sale, while the morning alert digest still featured it, so the objective covers every surface.
results.finding: Reader A (A3): 'The "so" does not follow at first reading; clause order hides the point.' The callback is compressed; the prose needs to say that the bike left search but not the digest, which is why the objective must cover every surface.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B B11 (the 'so' compresses a callback; re-read)

results.draft_locus: Journey SLOs: Defining Reliability Where Liquidity Is Made ¶4
results.quote: The brown-out alone spent about **30%** of Tradeyard NL's 28-day search budget in 48 minutes
results.finding: Reader A (A4): 'Had to check whether 30% fits 3.4 million failed; works only if many slow requests count, left implicit.'

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶1
results.quote: keep batch work out of peak windows with the peak calendar set out under capacity planning
results.finding: Reader A (A5): the calendar is leaned on by this sentence, the Figure 3 caption and isolation rule 1 before it is introduced two sections later; 'for a while the reader is told about a mechanism not yet met.' The spec's order (control points before capacity, calendar defined under capacity) creates the forward reference; both readers propose introducing the calendar earlier or defining it at first use.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B B4 (met three times before learning what it is)

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶2
results.quote: The first control point is the edge, where automated traffic is classified, and policy for it starts from why bots come.
results.finding: Reader A (A6): the first sentence joins two ideas awkwardly, and the subsection drifts into commercial, trust-and-safety and legal territory (Product design and Legal rows, AI-crawler licensing) that feels out of place in a section on control points in the search path. The material sits here by the spec's placement of p40/p41 (moved in round 3); the awkward opening sentence is a draft matter.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶4
results.quote: Behind the edge, the brown-out happened because interactive queries, reindexing and cache warm-up shared the same nodes at the same time.
results.finding: Reader A (A7): 'As written it says the brown-out happened behind the edge; reads oddly.'

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶6
results.quote: OLX is reported to have published a two-part post in 2021 on load shedding with NGINX using adaptive concurrency control; it could not be retrieved or verified for this book, so treat it as a pointer, not evidence.
results.finding: Reader A (A8): 'Unverified pointer interrupts the argument.' The spec lists this unretrievable OLX post as the paragraph's evidence, so the draft cannot drop it without a spec change.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B B5 (research note left in text; breaks flow)

results.draft_locus: Capacity Planning for Known Peaks ¶2
results.quote: Figures here count queries, meaning results-page requests; each query fans out to about 2.6 engine requests at Tradeyard
results.finding: Reader A (A9): 'Searches', 'queries' and 'requests' drift across the chapter (3.4 million failed search requests, 7 billion search requests, cost per thousand searches, cost per 1,000 queries, peak search requests at origin ~13,000/s); 'could not always tell what a figure counts.' The definition here is not held to elsewhere.

results.draft_locus: Capacity Planning for Known Peaks ¶4

results.quote: and only about 6% of the total from verified search engine crawlers
